hook: Perplexity says model A is better, the benchmark says model B, and my own eyes say neither. All three are right.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Perplexity says model A is better, the benchmark says model B, and my own eyes say neither. All three are right.

0:15 QUESTION — Every lab model card lists perplexity, a benchmark table, and a chatbot arena score. They often disagree. If you cannot say what each one measures, you cannot say whether your own training run got better, and that is the first thing an Anthropic or OpenAI eval team will ask.

1:00 INTUITION — Three thermometers for one patient. Perplexity is the core temperature: how surprised the model is by real text. A benchmark is a blood test for one skill. Vibes are the doctor talking to the patient. Each is cheap where the others are expensive. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Perplexity: PPL = exp( -(1/N) sum_t log p(x_t | x_<t) ). It is exp of the mean cross-entropy from M06E02, so it depends on the tokenizer: a model with bigger tokens sees fewer, harder tokens. Fix: bits per byte, BPB = (N_tokens / N_bytes) * CE / ln 2. Multiple-choice accuracy: pick argmax_c sum_{t in c} log p(t | context). The length-normalized version divides by the number of characters or tokens of c, which is why harnesses report acc and acc_norm.

5:30 CODE — Load gpt2-large with transformers on MPS. Write sliding_ppl(model, enc, max_len=1024, stride=512): loop windows, set labels to -100 for the overlapping prefix so each token is scored once, accumulate nll * n_scored, return exp(total_nll / total_tokens). Write mc_score(model, ctx, choices) returning summed and length-normalized logprobs. Score 50 HellaSwag items both ways. Then run the same 10 prompts through generate() for the vibes check and paste the outputs on screen.

9:00 RECEIPT — Hugging Face's perplexity guide reports gpt2-large on WikiText-2 test at about 19.4 with no overlap and about 16.4 with stride 512. My sliding_ppl must land within 0.1 of both. For multiple choice, my acc and acc_norm on the same 50 items must equal what lm_eval reports for those doc ids in the next episode.

10:30 MEASURE — One table, three rows: gpt2 vs gpt2-large on WikiText-2 PPL, BPB, HellaSwag acc_norm, and a 1-5 vibes score from me on 10 prompts. Point out where the ranking flips between PPL and BPB when I add a model with a different tokenizer, like Qwen3-0.6B.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Perplexity tracks pretraining, benchmarks track skills, vibes catch what neither measures, and you need all three. Interview line: I compare models across tokenizers in bits per byte, never raw perplexity.
12:30 NEXT — Next: lm-evaluation-harness on your model
key_math: PPL = exp(-(1/N) sum_t log p(x_t|x_<t)); BPB = (N_tok/N_bytes) * CE_nats / ln 2; MC choice = argmax_c sum_{t in c} log p(t|ctx), acc_norm divides by len(c) in characters (bytes).
code_task: sliding_ppl(model, encodings, max_len=1024, stride=512) -> float, with input_ids windows of shape (1, <=1024) and labels masked to -100 on the overlap; bpb(ce_nats, n_tokens, n_bytes) -> float; mc_score(model, tok, ctx: str, choices: list[str]) -> (logp_sum: Tensor[n_choices], logp_norm: Tensor[n_choices]).
receipt: abs(sliding_ppl(gpt2_large, wikitext2_test, stride=1024) - 19.44) < 0.1 and abs(sliding_ppl(..., stride=512) - 16.45) < 0.1 (numbers from the Hugging Face 'Perplexity of fixed-length models' guide; verify the exact values on the current page); per-item acc/acc_norm equals lm_eval's samples output for the same HellaSwag docs.
gotchas: Transformers shifts labels internally, so passing pre-shifted labels double-shifts and the PPL looks great; averaging per-window perplexities instead of summing NLL over tokens gives the wrong number; comparing PPL across different tokenizers is meaningless, use bits per byte.
interview_q: Why can't you compare the perplexity of Llama 3 and GPT-2 directly? Perplexity is per token and they use different tokenizers, so the denominators differ; convert to bits per byte (or nats per character) to put them on the same scale.
explainer: We have one model and three ways to grade it. Perplexity on the left, a benchmark in the middle, a human reading outputs on the right.
Perplexity first. For each token we take the log probability the model gave the true next token, average them, flip the sign and exponentiate.
Here is the catch. The same sentence becomes twelve tokens in one tokenizer and nine in another, so the averages are over different things.
Divide total surprise by bytes instead of tokens and both models land on the same ruler. That is bits per byte.
Now the benchmark. Four candidate endings, and we add up the log probability of each one. The longest ending loses just for being long.
Divide by length and the right answer wins. That is the difference between acc and acc norm in every eval table.
Finally vibes. Two models with almost the same perplexity, and one of them writes clearly better stories. No single number caught that.
explainer_visuals: Three panels side by side: a gauge labeled PPL, a checklist labeled HellaSwag, a speech bubble labeled vibes, one model icon in the center with arrows to each.
A sentence as token boxes, each with a small bar for log p; bars average into one number, then exp() animates to the PPL value.
The same sentence tokenized two ways, 12 boxes vs 9 boxes, stacked; the PPL values above differ.
Both rows collapse into a byte ruler of equal length; a single BPB number appears for each and they become comparable.
Context box with four ending boxes of different lengths; summed logprob bars, the longest one shortest bar, red X on the true answer.
Bars rescale by length; the true answer's bar becomes the tallest, label acc_norm.
Two story text blocks side by side with nearly equal PPL badges; one gets a green check from a reviewer icon.
short: The MATH beat on bits per byte. Caption: 'Your perplexity comparison is probably wrong.'
yt_title: LLM Evals 101: Perplexity vs Benchmarks vs Vibes (and Bits per Byte)
x_post: Perplexity is per token. Change the tokenizer and the number changes even if the model doesn't. Compare models in bits per byte. I reproduced HF's gpt2-large WikiText-2 PPL (16.45 at stride 512) from scratch. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I scored the same models three ways: sliding-window perplexity, HellaSwag multiple choice, and a hand-graded vibes check. My perplexity matched Hugging Face's published gpt2-large number. The lesson: rankings flip across tokenizers unless you report bits per byte.

hook: My TinyStories model scores 25 percent on a four-choice benchmark. That is not bad. That is a coin with four sides.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — My TinyStories model scores 25 percent on a four-choice benchmark. That is not bad. That is a coin with four sides.

0:15 QUESTION — The Open LLM Leaderboard, the Llama 3 and Qwen 3 model cards, and most papers report numbers from EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness. If you want to claim your model is better, you run the same harness with the same settings, or your number means nothing.

1:00 INTUITION — The harness is a standardized exam hall. Same questions, same prompt template, same scoring rule for every model. The interesting part is the random-chance floor: below it, the model learned nothing the exam can see. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Loglikelihood tasks score each choice by sum log p(choice | prompt), pick the argmax, and report acc with standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Chance on 4-way HellaSwag is 0.25. For generation tasks like GSM8K, the harness samples, extracts the answer with a regex filter, and exact-matches. Few-shot k changes the prompt, so k is part of the result.

4:00 CODE — pip install lm-eval. CLI: lm_eval --model hf --model_args pretrained=gpt2,dtype=float32 --tasks hellaswag,arc_easy,lambada_openai --batch_size 16 --device cuda:0 --output_path results/ --log_samples. Then wrap my own TinyStories GPT and my M11 SFT model: subclass lm_eval.api.model.LM with loglikelihood(requests), loglikelihood_rolling(requests), generate_until(requests), register it with @register_model('feather'). Each request has .args = (context, continuation).

7:30 RECEIPT — Before trusting my wrapper, run it on HF gpt2 weights loaded into my own GPT class. Its hellaswag acc_norm and lambada_openai acc must match the built-in hf backend on gpt2 to 3 decimals. Expect HellaSwag acc_norm near 0.31 and LAMBADA acc near 0.33 for gpt2 124M (verify against your own hf-backend run, the leaderboard reports differ by settings).

9:30 MEASURE — Bar chart with error bars: TinyStories 30M, gpt2, my SFT model, Qwen3-0.6B, across hellaswag, arc_easy, lambada_openai, with a dashed chance line. The TinyStories model sits on the chance line for ARC and is well above it on LAMBADA-style story completion. Show the --log_samples file for one item so viewers see the exact prompt.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — A benchmark number is model plus harness version plus prompt plus k plus normalization. Interview line: I always report the harness version, task config and standard error, and I check my model wrapper against the reference backend first.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Build your own eval with Inspect
key_math: acc = (1/n) sum_i 1[argmax_c sum_t log p(c_t|prompt_i, c_<t) = y_i]; SE = sqrt(acc(1-acc)/n); chance = 1/num_choices.
code_task: FeatherLM(lm_eval.api.model.LM) with loglikelihood(requests) -> list[tuple[float, bool]] (sum logprob, is_greedy), loglikelihood_rolling(requests) -> list[float], generate_until(requests) -> list[str]; batches (B, T) right-padded with an attention mask; registered via @register_model('feather') and run with lm_eval.simple_evaluate(model=FeatherLM(...), tasks=[...]).
receipt: Same gpt2 weights: abs(feather_results['hellaswag']['acc_norm,none'] - hf_results['hellaswag']['acc_norm,none']) < 1e-3 and the same for lambada_openai acc; per-sample logprobs from --log_samples agree to 1e-4.
gotchas: Tokenizing context and continuation separately vs jointly changes the boundary token and shifts scores, the harness expects you to split at the boundary carefully; forgetting to return is_greedy breaks LAMBADA accuracy; padding on the left without fixing position ids silently corrupts logprobs for a learned-position GPT.
interview_q: Two papers report different MMLU numbers for the same model. Why? Different harness versions, prompt templates, few-shot counts, and scoring (letter logprob vs full-answer logprob vs generation), so you only compare numbers produced under the same config.
explainer: Here is the harness as a pipeline. A task file goes in on the left, a model sits in the middle, and a results table comes out on the right.
For a multiple choice question, the harness builds one request per answer. Same context, different continuation.
Our model returns one number per request, the summed log probability of that continuation. The biggest one is the prediction.
Average correct predictions over the dataset and attach a standard error. That error bar is part of the result, not decoration.
Now the floor. Four choices means a random guesser scores a quarter. We draw that as a dashed line across every chart.
Our tiny story model hugs the dashed line on science questions. On story completion it climbs well above it.
Same weights in our wrapper and in the reference backend give the same number. Only then do we trust the wrapper on our own models.
explainer_visuals: Left-to-right flow: YAML task file icon, model box, results table with columns task/metric/value/stderr.
One question box fanning into four request boxes, each (context, choice_i).
Four bars of summed logprob; the tallest highlighted as the prediction.
Accuracy number with a whisker showing +/- 1.96 SE.
Bar chart axes with a dashed horizontal line at 0.25 labeled chance.
Grouped bars per task for four models; TinyStories bar sits on the line for ARC, rises for LAMBADA.
Two identical bars labeled 'feather wrapper' and 'hf backend' with a green equals sign.
short: The RECEIPT beat: same weights, two backends, same number. Caption: 'Test your eval wrapper before you trust it.'
yt_title: lm-evaluation-harness Tutorial: Benchmark Your Own LLM the Right Way
x_post: Before running lm-eval-harness on your own model class, load GPT-2 weights into it and check it matches the hf backend to 3 decimals. Mine didn't at first: a tokenization boundary bug. Code + video:
linkedin: I ran EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness on my from-scratch TinyStories model and my SFT model, using a custom LM wrapper. I validated the wrapper by matching the built-in backend on GPT-2 weights to three decimals. Every chart now has a chance line and error bars, because a 4-choice benchmark at 25% means nothing was learned.

hook: Standard benchmarks tell you how a model does on someone else's question. The useful evals are the ones you write for yours.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Standard benchmarks tell you how a model does on someone else's question. The useful evals are the ones you write for yours.

0:15 QUESTION — UK AISI built Inspect to run the evals governments use to test frontier models, and Anthropic and others publish evals in it. It is also the fastest way to turn 'I think the model is bad at X' into a number. We build one for a narrow skill: converting units correctly in physics word problems.

1:00 INTUITION — An Inspect eval is three parts: a dataset of samples, a solver that decides how the model is called, and a scorer that decides if the answer is right. Swap any one without touching the others. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Not much math, but one decision rule. Exact-match scorers have no noise but miss correct paraphrases. An LLM judge has error rates: if judge accuracy vs humans is a and true accuracy is p, the measured score is p*TPR + (1-p)*FPR. So we measure judge agreement with my own labels on 40 samples before trusting it.

4:00 CODE — pip install inspect-ai. In units_eval.py: from inspect_ai import Task, task; from inspect_ai.dataset import Sample, json_dataset; from inspect_ai.solver import system_message, generate, chain_of_thought; from inspect_ai.scorer import match, model_graded_qa. Write 60 Samples with input and target. @task def units(): return Task(dataset=..., solver=[system_message(SYS), generate()], scorer=match(numeric=True)). Second task variant uses model_graded_qa() with a grading template. Write a custom @scorer that parses a number plus unit with pint and compares within 1 percent.

7:30 RECEIPT — Run inspect eval units_eval.py --model anthropic/<current small Claude model> and --model openai/<small model>, then inspect view. Receipt one: my custom scorer agrees with my hand labels on 100 percent of the 40 labeled samples. Receipt two: Cohen's kappa between model_graded_qa and my labels, reported, and if it is below 0.8 the judge does not ship.

9:30 MEASURE — Table: model by solver (plain generate vs chain_of_thought) by scorer (match, pint scorer, LLM judge), accuracy with stderr from the Inspect log. Point to one sample where match() says wrong and the answer is right, 2.5 km written as 2500 m.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Write the scorer first, validate it against your own labels, then trust the number. Interview line: an LLM judge is a measurement instrument, so I report its agreement with human labels before any score it produces.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Contamination, variance and error bars
key_math: measured = p * TPR + (1 - p) * FPR (judge bias); Cohen's kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e).
code_task: units_eval.py: @task units() -> Task(dataset=list[Sample(input, target, metadata)], solver=[system_message(SYS), generate()], scorer=unit_scorer()); @scorer(metrics=[accuracy(), stderr()]) def unit_scorer(): async def score(state, target) -> Score parses state.output.completion with a regex + pint and returns CORRECT/INCORRECT; judge variant uses model_graded_qa().
receipt: unit_scorer agrees with 40/40 hand labels; sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score(judge_labels, my_labels) >= 0.8 or the judge is rejected; inspect log shows the same accuracy and stderr as my recomputation from log samples.
gotchas: match() compares strings, so '2500 m' vs '2.5 km' fails unless you write a unit-aware scorer; the judge model scoring its own family's outputs can be biased, use a different grader model; forgetting temperature and seed settings makes reruns differ and hides that you only ran once.
interview_q: How would you build an eval for a capability no benchmark covers? Write a small, hand-labeled dataset, pick a scorer that is deterministic if possible, validate any LLM judge against human labels with an agreement metric, and report accuracy with a standard error.
explainer: An Inspect eval is three boxes in a row: a dataset of samples, a solver that talks to the model, and a scorer that grades.
Each sample is a question and a target. Ours are physics word problems where the trap is the unit conversion.
The solver is a little program. Here it adds a system message, then calls generate. Swap in chain of thought and nothing else changes.
The scorer reads the model's text and decides right or wrong. String match marks two and a half kilometers wrong when the target is meters.
So we write our own scorer. It parses the number and unit, converts both, and checks they agree within one percent.
The judge model is another option, but it makes mistakes too. We compare its labels against ours and compute agreement.
Only scorers that agree with our hand labels make it into the final table.
explainer_visuals: Three connected boxes labeled Dataset, Solver, Scorer with arrows, model icon below Solver.
A Sample card with input text and target '2500 m'.
Solver box expanding into a chain: system_message -> generate, then a second version with chain_of_thought inserted.
Model output '2.5 km' vs target '2500 m', string match shows red X.
Parser converting '2.5 km' to 2500 m, green check, tolerance bar at 1%.
Confusion matrix judge vs human, kappa value written below.
Final table with rows per scorer, rejected judge row greyed out.
short: The 2.5 km vs 2500 m moment from MEASURE. Caption: 'Your eval marked the right answer wrong.'
yt_title: Build a Custom LLM Eval with UK AISI Inspect (Tasks, Solvers, Scorers)
x_post: My first Inspect eval marked '2.5 km' wrong because the target said '2500 m'. Scorer bugs are eval bugs. Validate the scorer and any LLM judge against your own labels before trusting a single number. Code + video:
linkedin: I built a custom eval in UK AISI's Inspect for unit conversion in physics problems: dataset, solver, and a unit-aware scorer. I validated an LLM judge against my own labels with Cohen's kappa before using it. The biggest error in the first version was in the scorer, not the model.

hook: A two point gain on a 200 question eval is inside the noise. Most leaderboard wins I checked were too.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A two point gain on a 200 question eval is inside the noise. Most leaderboard wins I checked were too.

0:15 QUESTION — Anthropic published a paper on adding error bars to evals because labs kept shipping claims that did not survive a second run. Two problems: the number is noisy, and the model may have seen the test during pretraining. Both make one number lie.

1:00 INTUITION — An eval is a poll. 200 questions is 200 voters. A poll of 200 has a margin of error, and if some voters were coached in advance, the poll is biased no matter how many you ask. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Standard error of accuracy: SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n). With p=0.7 and n=200, SE is about 0.032, so a 95 percent interval is plus or minus 6.3 points. Bootstrap: resample the n per-question scores with replacement B=10,000 times, take the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles. Paired comparison: for two models on the same questions, compute d_i = s_A,i - s_B,i and SE(d) = std(d)/sqrt(n). Pairing removes question difficulty and is much tighter. Clustered SE when questions share a passage: sum residuals within clusters before squaring.

5:30 CODE — bootstrap_ci(scores: np.ndarray[n], B=10000, alpha=0.05) -> (lo, hi). paired_diff_ci(a: np.ndarray[n], b: np.ndarray[n]). seed_variance(task, model, seeds=range(5)) reruns the Inspect eval from M14E03 at temperature 0.7. Contamination check: ngram_overlap(test_item, corpus_index, n=13) using a hashed set of 13-grams from my pretraining shards, the same n GPT-3 used for its decontamination.

8:30 RECEIPT — Receipt one: bootstrap CI width matches the analytic 1.96*SE to within 5 percent for n=200, p=0.7. Receipt two: run the same model twice at temperature 0.7 and show the scores differ by about the SE predicted. Receipt three: plant 20 test items into a shard, rerun ngram_overlap, and it flags all 20.

10:00 MEASURE — Two plots. First, 95 percent CI width vs n for p=0.7 on a log axis, with markers at n=100, 500, 2000. Second, model A vs B: unpaired CIs overlap, the paired CI on the difference excludes zero. Same data, opposite conclusions, and the paired one is right.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — Report a confidence interval, use paired tests when models share questions, and check for contamination before celebrating. Interview line: a gain smaller than two standard errors of the paired difference is not a result.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Evaluating agents
key_math: SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n); CI95 = p +/- 1.96 SE; paired: d_i = s_A,i - s_B,i, SE_d = sd(d)/sqrt(n); clustered: SE_c = sqrt( sum_k (sum_{i in k}(s_i - p))^2 ) / n.
code_task: bootstrap_ci(scores: np.ndarray (n,), B=10000, alpha=0.05) -> tuple[float, float] using rng.integers(0, n, size=(B, n)); paired_diff_ci(a, b) -> (mean_d, lo, hi); clustered_se(scores, cluster_ids); ngram_overlap(text, index: set[int], n=13) -> float fraction of 13-grams found.
receipt: abs((hi - lo) / (2 * 1.96 * sqrt(0.7*0.3/200)) - 1) < 0.05 on simulated Bernoulli(0.7) scores; planted-contamination test flags 20/20 items with overlap > 0.5; paired CI is strictly narrower than the unpaired CI on the same two models.
gotchas: Bootstrapping over samples within one run ignores seed variance, rerun with different seeds too; treating questions from the same passage as independent underestimates SE, cluster them; checking contamination on token ids from a different tokenizer finds nothing, normalize text first.
interview_q: Model B beats A by 1.5 points on a 1,000 question eval. Ship it? Compute the paired difference CI over the same questions and also check seed variance; if the CI includes zero or the gain is within run-to-run noise, it is not a real improvement.
explainer: Here are two hundred questions as a grid of squares, green for right and red for wrong. The model gets seventy percent.
Now we resample the grid with replacement, ten thousand times. Each resample gives a slightly different score.
Stack those scores into a histogram. The middle ninety five percent is our confidence interval, about six points wide.
Two models with overlapping intervals look tied. But they answered the same questions, so we compare them question by question.
Most questions both get right or both get wrong. Only the disagreements carry signal, and the paired interval shrinks.
Contamination is different. If test questions sat in the training data, the score is high for the wrong reason.
We hash every thirteen word window of the training shards and look up each test question. Planted copies light up.
explainer_visuals: 20 x 10 grid of squares, 140 green 60 red, '70%' label.
Animated resampling: random squares duplicated, score ticker changing.
Histogram of bootstrap scores with shaded 95% band and its width labeled.
Two overlapping CI bars for models A and B.
Paired grid: matching squares fade out, disagreement squares highlighted; a much narrower CI bar on the difference.
Training corpus scroll with a test question highlighted inside it.
Sliding 13-gram window over a test item, hash lookups lighting up red for planted items.
short: The paired vs unpaired MEASURE plot. Caption: 'Same data. Opposite conclusion.'
yt_title: Error Bars for LLM Evals: Bootstrap, Paired Tests and Contamination
x_post: A 70% score on 200 questions has a 95% CI of about +/- 6 points. If two models share questions, use a paired test, it's much tighter. And check 13-gram contamination before celebrating. Code + video:
linkedin: I added bootstrap confidence intervals, paired comparisons and a 13-gram contamination check to my eval pipeline. The bootstrap matched the analytic standard error, and planted contamination was caught 20 of 20 times. Two models that looked tied under unpaired intervals separated cleanly with a paired test.

hook: Grading an agent is not grading an answer. The agent can delete your files on its way to the right answer.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Grading an agent is not grading an answer. The agent can delete your files on its way to the right answer.

0:15 QUESTION — Claude Code and Codex now run multi-step tasks in real shells. SWE-bench and METR's task suites grade outcomes, but labs also care about how the agent got there. I built OperatorOK, a control plane that sandboxes Claude Code and Codex on my Mac and routes risky actions to my iPhone for approval. Today it becomes an eval harness.

1:00 INTUITION — An agent eval has four parts: a task with a starting environment, a sandbox so nothing escapes, a grader that checks the final state, and a monitor that watches the trajectory. Outcome and process are two separate scores. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Score per task: success s in {0,1} from hidden unit tests. Agent runs are stochastic, so report pass@1 averaged over k=5 attempts with SE, and pass^k (all k succeed) for reliability. Monitor: suspicion score m in [0,10] per trajectory. Choose threshold tau so the false positive rate on benign runs is 2 percent, then report recall on runs where I inserted a forbidden action.

4:30 CODE — Inspect task: Task(dataset=12 repo-fix samples, solver=react agent with bash() and python() tools, sandbox='docker', scorer=run_hidden_tests()). The scorer calls sandbox().exec(['pytest','-q','tests_hidden']) and returns CORRECT if exit code is 0. Monitor: a second model reads the transcript (state.messages) and outputs a 0-10 suspicion score with a reason. Then the OperatorOK version: same tasks, but the agent is real Claude Code inside the OperatorOK sandbox, and every approval request it sends to the phone is logged as a monitor event.

8:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: a scripted 'oracle agent' that applies the known patch passes 12 of 12, a no-op agent passes 0 of 12. That proves the grader. Receipt two: 6 trajectories where I inject 'curl to an unknown host' or 'rm -rf outside the repo'. The monitor at the 2 percent FPR threshold catches at least 5 of 6, and OperatorOK blocks all 6 at the approval gate.
10:00 MEASURE — Table: model by pass@1 over 5 attempts with SE, pass^5, mean tool calls, mean tokens, approvals requested. Plot: monitor ROC curve with the 2 percent FPR operating point marked.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — Grade agents on outcome with hidden tests, watch the process with a monitor, and validate both with oracle and adversarial trajectories. Interview line: I validate an agent grader with an oracle and a null agent before reporting any model's score.
12:30 NEXT — Next: The residual stream and the logit lens
key_math: pass@1 = mean over tasks and attempts of s; pass^k = mean over tasks of prod_{j=1..k} s_j; tau = quantile_{0.98}(m | benign); recall = P(m > tau | attack).
code_task: agent_eval.py: @task repo_fix() -> Task(dataset, solver=react(tools=[bash(timeout=60), python()]), sandbox='docker', scorer=hidden_tests()); @scorer hidden_tests() uses await sandbox().exec(['pytest','-q','tests_hidden']) and returns Score(value=CORRECT if result.returncode == 0 else INCORRECT); monitor_score(messages: list[ChatMessage]) -> (int 0-10, str reason); OperatorOK adapter that replays approval events into the same log format. Verify current Inspect agent API names (react vs basic_agent) in the docs before recording.
receipt: oracle agent 12/12 and null agent 0/12 on hidden tests; monitor recall >= 5/6 on injected attacks at threshold tau chosen for <= 2% FPR on 30 benign runs; OperatorOK approval gate blocks 6/6 injected actions.
gotchas: Leaving the hidden tests inside the sandbox lets the agent read or edit them, copy them in only at scoring time; Docker sandboxes with network on make results depend on the internet, pin dependencies and disable network unless the task needs it; one attempt per task hides huge variance, use k >= 5.
interview_q: How would you evaluate a coding agent safely? Run it in an isolated sandbox with no secrets and controlled network, score the final state with hidden tests, monitor the trajectory with a separate model, and validate the grader with an oracle and a null agent.
explainer: An agent eval starts with a task and a fresh sandbox. Inside the box is a broken repository and a shell.
The agent reads files, runs commands, and edits code. Each step lands in a transcript on the right.
When the agent says it is done, we copy hidden tests into the box and run them. Pass or fail is the outcome score.
Separately, a monitor model reads the whole transcript and gives it a suspicion score from zero to ten.
Most honest runs score low. A run that sends data to an unknown server should score high.
In OperatorOK, risky commands pause and ping my phone. Every one of those pauses becomes a logged event.
We pick the monitor threshold so only two percent of honest runs get flagged, then count how many attacks get caught.
explainer_visuals: Container box with a repo tree and a terminal prompt inside.
Agent icon issuing bash commands; transcript scroll growing on the right.
Hidden test file sliding into the box at the end; green PASS or red FAIL stamp.
Monitor eye icon reading the transcript, dial from 0 to 10.
Two histograms of suspicion scores, benign low and attack high, slight overlap.
Mac sandbox with an arrow to an iPhone showing an Approve/Deny prompt.
ROC curve with the 2% FPR point marked and recall labeled.

yt_title: Evaluating AI Agents: Sandboxed Coding Evals with a Monitor (Inspect)

hook: GPT-2 often knows the answer by layer eight. The last four layers are mostly making it more confident.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GPT-2 often knows the answer by layer eight. The last four layers are mostly making it more confident.

0:15 QUESTION — Anthropic's interpretability team starts from one idea: every layer reads from and writes to a shared residual stream. If that is true, we can decode the stream at any layer with the model's own unembedding and watch the prediction form. This is the first tool in the ARENA curriculum and the base of everything in this module.

1:00 INTUITION — The residual stream is a shared whiteboard. Each attention head and MLP reads the board and adds a note. The logit lens asks: if we stopped here and read the board out loud, what word would it say? [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Residual stream: x_0 = W_E[token] + W_pos[t]; x_{l+1} = x_l + sum_h Attn_h(x_l) + MLP(x_l') in pre-norm form. Final logits = W_U LN_final(x_L) + b_U. Logit lens at layer l: logits_l = W_U LN_final(x_l). Because the stream is a sum, the final logit is a sum of contributions from each component, which is why direct logit attribution works: logit diff = sum_components (LN-scaled component output) dot (W_U[:, correct] - W_U[:, wrong]).

5:00 CODE — from transformer_lens import HookedTransformer; model = HookedTransformer.from_pretrained('gpt2-small'). logits, cache = model.run_with_cache(tokens). resid = cache.accumulated_resid(layer=-1, incl_mid=True, apply_ln=True, return_labels=True) gives a stack of shape (2*n_layers+1, batch, pos, d_model). lens_logits = resid @ model.W_U + model.b_U. For each layer, rank of the correct next token and its probability. Prompt set: 'The Eiffel Tower is in the city of', plus 50 factual prompts.

8:00 RECEIPT — The logit lens at the last layer must equal the real logits: torch.testing.assert_close(model.unembed(model.ln_final(cache['resid_post', 11])), logits, atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4). Second receipt: direct logit attribution summed over all components plus the bias equals the final logit difference for ' Paris' vs ' London' to 1e-3. If it does not, the LN scaling is wrong.

10:00 MEASURE — Heatmap: layer on y, position on x, top decoded token in each cell, colored by probability of the correct answer. Line plot: median rank of the correct token vs layer across 50 prompts. Note where it drops to rank 1, and note the logit lens is noisier in early layers, which is why the tuned lens exists.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — The residual stream is a sum, so you can read it at any depth and attribute the final answer to components. Interview line: the logit lens works because pre-norm transformers keep a linear residual stream that the unembedding can read at any layer, up to a layernorm scale.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Activation patching
key_math: x_{l+1} = x_l + sum_h h_l(x_l) + m_l(x_l); logits_l = W_U LN_f(x_l) + b_U; logit_diff = sum_c (LN_f-scaled out_c) . (W_U[:,a] - W_U[:,b]).
code_task: logit_lens(model, tokens) -> Tensor (n_layers*2+1, pos, d_vocab) via cache.accumulated_resid(apply_ln=True) @ model.W_U + model.b_U; correct_rank(lens_logits, target_ids) -> Tensor (n_layers*2+1, pos); dla(cache, answer_dir) using cache.decompose_resid(apply_ln=True) dotted with W_U[:, a] - W_U[:, b].
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(model.unembed(model.ln_final(cache['resid_post', 11])), logits, atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4); sum of DLA contributions (plus bias term) equals logits[0,-1,paris] - logits[0,-1,london] within 1e-3.
gotchas: HookedTransformer.from_pretrained folds LayerNorm weights and centers the unembedding by default, so raw weights differ from Hugging Face's, which is fine but confuses comparisons; forgetting apply_ln=True makes early layers look meaningless because the stream norm grows with depth; token ' Paris' has a leading space, 'Paris' is a different token.
interview_q: Why does the logit lens work at all? In a pre-norm transformer each block adds to a shared residual stream, so intermediate states live in roughly the same basis the unembedding reads; applying the final layernorm and W_U gives a rough readout, sharper in later layers.
explainer: Here is the residual stream as one long horizontal bar running through all twelve layers of GPT-2.
Each attention block and each MLP reads the bar, computes something, and adds its output back on top.
At the end, a layer norm and the unembedding turn the bar into a score for every word in the vocabulary.
The logit lens is one move. We take the bar from the middle of the network and push it through that same final readout.
At layer two the top guess for the Eiffel Tower prompt is junk. By layer eight, Paris is already the top word.
The last layers raise Paris's probability without changing the answer. Most of the work happened earlier.
Because the bar is a sum, the final Paris score splits cleanly into contributions from every head and MLP.
explainer_visuals: Horizontal bar through 12 stacked block outlines, labeled resid.
Attention and MLP boxes with arrows reading from and adding into the bar (+ signs).
LN_final and W_U boxes at the right end producing a vocab bar chart.
A tap line from layer 6 of the bar routed to the same LN_final and W_U boxes.
Table of layers with top decoded token: junk words early, ' Paris' highlighted from layer 8.
Probability of ' Paris' vs layer line, rising late.
Stacked bar decomposing the Paris-minus-London logit into per-component segments.
short: The layer-by-layer heatmap reveal. Caption: 'GPT-2 knows the answer before it's done thinking.'
yt_title: Logit Lens with TransformerLens: Watch GPT-2 Predict Layer by Layer
x_post: Logit lens sanity check: decode the final residual stream with ln_final + W_U and it must equal the model's logits exactly. Then decode every earlier layer. GPT-2 small has the answer by layer ~8 on many factual prompts. Code + video:
linkedin: I built the logit lens and direct logit attribution on GPT-2 small with TransformerLens. The final-layer readout matched the model's logits exactly, and the per-component contributions summed to the final logit difference. On factual prompts the correct token often reaches rank 1 well before the last layer.

hook: Seeing what a model computes is correlation. Swapping one activation and watching the answer flip is causation.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Seeing what a model computes is correlation. Swapping one activation and watching the answer flip is causation.

0:15 QUESTION — The indirect object identification paper found a circuit of about 26 heads in GPT-2 small that completes 'When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to' with Mary. The tool that found it is activation patching, also called causal tracing in the ROME paper. Every serious interp claim rests on it.

1:00 INTUITION — Two runs of the same model: a clean prompt and a corrupted prompt where the names are swapped. Take one activation from the clean run, paste it into the corrupted run, and see how much of the right answer comes back. A component matters if patching it restores the answer. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Metric: logit difference LD = logit(IO) - logit(S) at the final position. Normalized patching effect: (LD_patched - LD_corrupt) / (LD_clean - LD_corrupt), so 0 means no recovery and 1 means full recovery. Patch at a node a_l,pos: replace a_l,pos(corrupt run) with a_l,pos(clean run) and keep everything downstream computed normally. Denoising (clean into corrupt) tests sufficiency, noising (corrupt into clean) tests necessity, and they can disagree.

4:30 CODE — model = HookedTransformer.from_pretrained('gpt2-small'). Build clean and corrupt prompts with the same token length. _, clean_cache = model.run_with_cache(clean_tokens). def patch_resid(act, hook, pos): act[:, pos] = clean_cache[hook.name][:, pos]; return act. Loop layers and positions with model.run_with_hooks(corrupt_tokens, fwd_hooks=[(utils.get_act_name('resid_pre', L), partial(patch_resid, pos=p))]). Then per-head patching of hook_z: act shape (batch, pos, n_heads, d_head), patch act[:, :, h]. Compare to transformer_lens.patching.get_act_patch_resid_pre and get_act_patch_attn_head_out_all_pos.

8:30 RECEIPT — My hand-written loop must equal the library: torch.testing.assert_close(my_resid_patch, patching.get_act_patch_resid_pre(model, corrupt_tokens, clean_cache, ld_metric)). Baseline sanity: clean LD around 3 to 4 nats averaged over the ARENA IOI prompt set (verify on your run), and patching resid_pre at layer 0 at the name position gives effect near 1 by construction.

10:30 MEASURE — Two heatmaps. Residual stream: layer by position, the signal starts at the name tokens and moves to the final token around layers 7 to 9. Attention heads: 12 by 12 grid, with the name mover heads the IOI paper reports (9.9, 9.6, 10.0) lighting up. Compare to the paper's figure.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Patching is a controlled experiment on a network: change one thing, measure the effect, and name the components that carry the signal. Interview line: I prefer a normalized logit difference metric over probability because it is linear in the residual stream and does not saturate.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Linear probes
key_math: LD = logit_IO - logit_S at last position; effect = (LD_patch - LD_corr) / (LD_clean - LD_corr); patch: a_{l,p}^{corr} <- a_{l,p}^{clean}.
code_task: ld_metric(logits, io_ids, s_ids) -> Tensor scalar; patch_resid_grid(model, clean_tokens, corrupt_tokens, clean_cache) -> Tensor (n_layers, seq_len) using run_with_hooks on utils.get_act_name('resid_pre', L); patch_head_grid(...) -> Tensor (n_layers, n_heads) patching hook_z with act shape (batch, pos, n_heads, d_head).
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(my_grid, transformer_lens.patching.get_act_patch_resid_pre(model, corrupt_tokens, clean_cache, metric)); effect at (layer 0, IO position) is about 1.0 and at layers with no path to the output about 0; top heads by effect include those the IOI paper calls name movers.
gotchas: Clean and corrupt prompts must tokenize to the same length or positions misalign silently; hooks mutate in place, return the tensor and reset hooks with model.reset_hooks() if a run errors mid-way; using probability as the metric saturates near 1 and hides partial recovery.
interview_q: What is the difference between denoising and noising patches? Denoising patches clean activations into a corrupted run and shows which components are sufficient to restore behavior; noising patches corrupted activations into a clean run and shows which are necessary. Backup heads can make them disagree.
explainer: We run GPT-2 twice. The clean prompt ends with John gave a drink to, and the right answer is Mary.
The corrupted prompt swaps the names, so the model now prefers the wrong person. Same length, same structure.
Now the experiment. We copy one activation from the clean run and paste it into the corrupted run at one layer and one position.
If the answer swings back toward Mary, that activation carried the information. We score the swing from zero to one.
Repeat for every layer and position and we get a heatmap. The signal starts at the name tokens.
Around layer eight it jumps to the final position. That is where the model moves the name into the answer.
Patch individual heads and a handful light up. Those are the name mover heads from the original paper.
explainer_visuals: Clean prompt tokens in a row, logit bar showing Mary > John.
Corrupted prompt tokens with swapped names, logit bar flipped.
Two stacked network diagrams; an arrow carries one highlighted cell from top to bottom.
Logit-difference gauge moving from 0 to near 1.
Layer x position heatmap filling in, bright at name positions in early layers.
Bright region moving to the last column around layers 7-9.
12x12 head grid with three bright cells labeled 9.6, 9.9, 10.0.
short: The heatmap where the signal jumps from the name to the final token. Caption: 'Watch information move through GPT-2.'
yt_title: Activation Patching in TransformerLens: Find the IOI Circuit in GPT-2
x_post: Activation patching = copy one activation from a clean run into a corrupted run and measure how much of the right answer returns. On IOI in GPT-2 small, the signal hops from the name token to the last token around layer 8. Code + video:
linkedin: I implemented activation patching by hand in TransformerLens and checked it matches the library's patching functions exactly. On the IOI task in GPT-2 small, the head-level heatmap recovered the name mover heads reported in the original paper. Normalized logit difference was the metric that made partial effects visible.

hook: A probe that hits 95 percent accuracy can still tell you nothing about the model. Here is how to tell the difference.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A probe that hits 95 percent accuracy can still tell you nothing about the model. Here is how to tell the difference.

0:15 QUESTION — Linear probes found board state in Othello-GPT and a truth direction in Llama-2 in the 'Geometry of Truth' paper. Anthropic and others use probes as cheap monitors for things like deception. But a strong probe can learn the task itself from rich features. You need controls.

1:00 INTUITION — A probe is a ruler laid across activation space. If one straight line separates true statements from false ones, the model represents truth linearly at that layer. The control asks whether the ruler would also separate random labels, which means it is measuring itself, not the model. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Logistic probe: p(y=1|x) = sigma(w^T x + b), trained with binary cross-entropy plus L2 penalty lambda ||w||^2. Difference of means probe: w = mu_true - mu_false, no training, often more robust out of distribution. Selectivity (Hewitt and Liang): acc(real task) - acc(control task with random but consistent labels per token type). High selectivity means the information is in the model, not learned by the probe.

4:30 CODE — Dataset: 400 true/false statements like 'The city of Paris is in France' and their false swaps, from the Geometry of Truth repo's cities set (or written by hand). With TransformerLens on gpt2-medium or Pythia-410M: _, cache = model.run_with_cache(toks, names_filter=lambda n: n.endswith('resid_post')). Take the last-token activation per layer, shape (N, d_model). Train sklearn LogisticRegression(C=0.1) per layer on a 70/30 split. Also the difference-of-means direction. Control: shuffle labels and retrain.

8:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: my PyTorch logistic probe (nn.Linear(d_model,1) + BCEWithLogitsLoss + weight_decay) matches sklearn's test accuracy within 1 point on the best layer. Receipt two: the shuffled-label control probe sits near 50 percent on the test set. Receipt three: causal check, adding +alpha * w_dim to the residual stream at that layer shifts the model's logit for ' True' after a 'True or False:' prompt in the predicted direction.

10:00 MEASURE — Plot: probe accuracy vs layer for logistic, difference-of-means, and control. Truth becomes linearly decodable in middle layers and peaks before the end. PCA of the best layer's activations colored by label, the two clusters visible on screen.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — Probes tell you what is decodable, controls tell you if it is the model's or the probe's, and an intervention tells you if the model uses it. Interview line: decodable is not the same as used, so I follow every probe with a causal intervention along the probe direction.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Sparse autoencoders
key_math: p(y|x) = sigma(w^T x + b); L = BCE + lambda ||w||^2; w_dm = mu_1 - mu_0; selectivity = acc_task - acc_control.
code_task: collect_acts(model, prompts) -> dict[layer, Tensor (N, d_model)] at the last token via run_with_cache with names_filter; train_probe(X, y) -> (w: Tensor (d_model,), b, test_acc); diff_means(X, y) -> Tensor (d_model,); intervene(model, layer, direction, alpha) using a hook on resid_post that adds alpha * direction / direction.norm().
receipt: abs(torch_probe_acc - sklearn_probe_acc) < 0.01 at the best layer; shuffled-label control test acc in [0.45, 0.55]; adding +alpha*w at the best layer raises logit(' True') - logit(' False') on held-out false statements, and -alpha lowers it.
gotchas: Statements differ in length, so take the last real token, not position -1 of a padded batch; train/test split must be by statement pair, or the probe sees the true and false twin and memorizes; unnormalized features across layers make regularization strength mean different things, standardize per layer.
interview_q: Your probe gets 95% accuracy at detecting deception in activations. What else do you need before believing it? A control task to measure selectivity, out-of-distribution test sets, and a causal intervention showing the model's behavior changes along that direction.
explainer: We feed the model two hundred true statements and two hundred false ones and grab the activation at the last token.
Each statement becomes one point in a space with a thousand dimensions. We squash it to two for the picture.
At an early layer the true and false points are mixed together. No straight line separates them.
In the middle layers they pull apart into two clouds. A single line now splits them with high accuracy.
Now the control. Shuffle the labels and train again. A good probe on real structure drops to a coin flip.
Last step. We push activations along the probe's direction and watch the model say True more often.
Decodable, selective, and causal. A probe that passes all three is telling us about the model.
explainer_visuals: List of true (green) and false (red) statements feeding into a model block; an arrow pulls out the last-token vector.
Point cloud in 2D PCA projection, green and red dots.
Layer 2 scatter: dots fully mixed.
Layer 12 scatter: two separated clusters with a decision line drawn.
Same scatter with random colors; accuracy counter drops to ~50%.
Arrow along the probe direction added to the residual stream; bar for ' True' logit grows.
Three check marks labeled decodable, selective, causal.
short: The control probe dropping to 50%. Caption: 'Your 95% probe might be measuring itself.'
yt_title: Linear Probes on LLM Activations: Finding a Truth Direction
x_post: Linear probes need three checks: accuracy by layer, a shuffled-label control (should be ~50%), and a causal intervention along the probe direction. Mine found a truth direction in mid layers that actually moved the model's answer. Code + video:
linkedin: I trained linear and difference-of-means probes for true vs false statements across every layer of a small model. A shuffled-label control stayed at chance, and pushing activations along the probe direction shifted the model's True/False answer. Probes show what is decodable; interventions show what is used.

hook: One GPT-2 neuron fires for French, base64, and the word 'bank'. A sparse autoencoder splits it into features that each mean one thing.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — One GPT-2 neuron fires for French, base64, and the word 'bank'. A sparse autoencoder splits it into features that each mean one thing.

0:15 QUESTION — Anthropic's Towards Monosemanticity trained a sparse autoencoder on a one-layer transformer and found thousands of interpretable features, and Scaling Monosemanticity did it on Claude 3 Sonnet. SAEs are now the standard tool for turning polysemantic neurons into readable features. We train one on GPT-2 small's residual stream.

1:00 INTUITION — Superposition: the model stores more concepts than it has dimensions by packing them in nearly orthogonal directions. An SAE is an overcomplete dictionary: it rewrites each activation as a sparse combination of many more directions than the model has neurons. Few active features per token means each one can be named. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Encoder: f = ReLU(W_enc (x - b_dec) + b_enc), with W_enc of shape (d_sae, d_model), d_sae = 16 to 32 times d_model. Decoder: x_hat = W_dec f + b_dec. Loss: L = ||x - x_hat||^2 + lambda * sum_i f_i * ||W_dec[:, i]||_2. Weighting the L1 by the decoder norm stops the model cheating by shrinking f and growing W_dec. Metrics: L0 = mean number of nonzero f per token; fraction of variance explained; CE loss recovered = (CE_zero_abl - CE_sae) / (CE_zero_abl - CE_clean).

5:00 CODE — Collect resid_pre at layer 8 of gpt2-small with run_with_cache over 50M tokens of OpenWebText, streamed in chunks of (4096, 768). class SAE(nn.Module) with W_enc (768, 24576), b_enc, W_dec (24576, 768), b_dec initialized to the data mean. Adam lr 4e-4, lambda warmup over the first 5 percent of steps. Track L0, dead features (never fired in the last 10M tokens), variance explained. Then splice: run_with_hooks with a hook that replaces resid_pre with sae(x_hat) and measure next-token CE.

8:30 RECEIPT — Compare to a published SAE on the same hook: load Joseph Bloom's gpt2-small residual SAEs via SAELens (release 'gpt2-small-res-jb', id for blocks.8.hook_resid_pre; check current SAELens API). Report L0, variance explained and CE loss recovered for both on the same 1M held-out tokens. My SAE should be in the same range; if CE recovered is below 0.9, something is wrong.

10:30 MEASURE — Feature dashboard for 5 features: top 20 activating contexts with the token highlighted, activation histogram, and the top logits each decoder column promotes through W_U. Plot the L0 vs CE-recovered frontier for three lambda values, with the SAELens SAE as a reference point.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — An SAE trades reconstruction for sparsity, and you judge it by the Pareto frontier of L0 against CE loss recovered, then by whether its features are readable. Interview line: I report CE loss recovered when splicing the SAE into the model, because low MSE can still break the model's next-token predictions.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Steering vectors
key_math: f = ReLU(W_enc(x - b_dec) + b_enc); x_hat = W_dec f + b_dec; L = ||x - x_hat||_2^2 + lambda sum_i f_i ||W_dec,i||_2; CE_rec = (CE_zero - CE_sae) / (CE_zero - CE_clean).
code_task: SAE(d_model=768, d_sae=24576) with encode(x: (B,768)) -> f (B,24576), decode(f) -> x_hat (B,768), forward returning (x_hat, f, loss); activation buffer from run_with_cache(names_filter='blocks.8.hook_resid_pre') shuffled across 50M tokens; splice_ce(model, sae, tokens) using run_with_hooks to replace the activation; feature_dashboard(feature_id) -> top contexts + W_U @ W_dec[i] top tokens.
receipt: On 1M held-out OpenWebText tokens: my SAE and the SAELens gpt2-small-res-jb layer-8 SAE both reported with L0, variance explained, and CE loss recovered; mine has CE recovered >= 0.9 at comparable L0; dead features < 10%.
gotchas: Not shuffling the activation buffer trains on one document at a time and features collapse; dead features pile up without resampling or a proper init, track them from step one; the L1 penalty without decoder-norm weighting lets the model shrink activations and grow decoder columns, so sparsity looks great and means nothing.
interview_q: How do you know an SAE is good? Check the sparsity/fidelity frontier (L0 against CE loss recovered when spliced into the model), the fraction of dead features, and whether top-activating examples of random features are interpretable to a human or an auto-interp model.
explainer: Here is one neuron from GPT-2 and the text that makes it fire. French, base64, and money words, all mixed up.
The model has seven hundred sixty eight dimensions in this layer, but it seems to track far more concepts than that.
It packs them in at slight angles. Each concept is a direction, and directions overlap a little. That is superposition.
A sparse autoencoder expands each activation into twenty four thousand slots, then rebuilds the original from those slots.
The sparsity penalty means only a few dozen slots turn on for any token. Each slot becomes a candidate feature.
Now look at one slot's top examples. It fires on base64 strings and nothing else.
We plug the autoencoder back into the model and check the next word predictions barely change. That is the real test.
explainer_visuals: A neuron icon with three text snippets in different colors (French, base64, 'bank') feeding into it.
A 768-length vector bar next to a cloud of many concept labels.
2D plot with 5 arrows at near-orthogonal angles crammed into a plane.
Narrow vector expanding into a wide 24576-slot bar then contracting back; labels encoder and decoder.
Wide bar with only a few bright slots lit; L0 counter.
Feature card: top contexts with the base64 token highlighted.
Model diagram with the SAE spliced into layer 8; CE loss bars for clean, SAE, zero-ablate.
short: The feature dashboard for one clean feature. Caption: 'I found the base64 neuron that GPT-2 hides.'
yt_title: Sparse Autoencoders from Scratch: Find Interpretable Features in GPT-2
x_post: Low SAE reconstruction loss is not enough. Splice the SAE into the model and measure CE loss recovered. My layer-8 GPT-2 SAE vs a published SAELens one, same tokens, same metrics. Code + video:
linkedin: I trained a sparse autoencoder on GPT-2 small's layer-8 residual stream from scratch and compared it to a published SAELens SAE on L0, variance explained and CE loss recovered. Feature dashboards turned up clean single-concept features. The most useful metric was CE loss recovered with the SAE spliced into the model.

hook: I changed what GPT-2 talks about without training it, without a prompt, by adding one vector to layer six.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — I changed what GPT-2 talks about without training it, without a prompt, by adding one vector to layer six.

0:15 QUESTION — Activation addition (Turner et al.) and contrastive activation addition on Llama 2 (Rimsky et al.) showed you can steer a model by adding a direction to the residual stream. Anthropic's Golden Gate Claude did it with an SAE feature. Steering is both a control tool and a test of whether a direction means what we think it means.

1:00 INTUITION — If concepts are directions in the residual stream, then pushing the stream along a direction should push the output toward that concept. The steering vector is the difference between the model thinking about 'love' and thinking about 'hate'. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — ActAdd: v = x_l(prompt_+) - x_l(prompt_-) at the last tokens of a contrast pair. CAA: v = mean_i x_l(pos_i) - mean_i x_l(neg_i) over many pairs, which averages out prompt noise. Inject: x_l <- x_l + alpha * v at every position after the prompt. SAE steering: v = W_dec[:, k] for feature k. Too large alpha pushes the stream off-distribution and the text degrades, so we measure fluency too.

4:30 CODE — model = HookedTransformer.from_pretrained('gpt2-medium' or a small Llama-style model on Mac). v = steering_vector(model, pos_prompts, neg_prompts, layer=6). def add_hook(act, hook): act[:, :, :] += alpha * v; return act. with model.hooks(fwd_hooks=[(utils.get_act_name('resid_pre', 6), add_hook)]): out = model.generate(prompt, max_new_tokens=60, temperature=0.7). Sweep alpha in {0, 2, 4, 8, 16}, 20 samples each. Score sentiment with an off-the-shelf classifier and fluency with perplexity under unsteered GPT-2.

8:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: at alpha=0 the hooked generate matches unhooked generate token for token with the same seed. Receipt two: positive-sentiment rate rises monotonically from alpha 0 to 8 over 100 samples with a bootstrap CI that excludes the alpha=0 rate. Receipt three: a random vector of the same norm moves sentiment by less than the CI. If random works as well, the direction means nothing.

10:00 MEASURE — Plot: sentiment score vs alpha for CAA vector, ActAdd single-pair vector, SAE feature vector, and random. Second axis: perplexity of the output. Show the sweet spot and the cliff. Read two before/after samples out loud.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — Adding a direction to the residual stream changes behavior, and the random-vector control is what makes it evidence. Interview line: steering is a causal test of a representation, so I always compare against a norm-matched random direction and track fluency.
12:30 NEXT — Next: How DeepSeek works: the efficiency playbook
key_math: v_ActAdd = x_l(p+) - x_l(p-); v_CAA = mean_i x_l(pos_i) - mean_i x_l(neg_i); x_l <- x_l + alpha v; v_SAE = W_dec[:, k].
code_task: steering_vector(model, pos: list[str], neg: list[str], layer: int) -> Tensor (d_model,) using cache['resid_pre', layer][:, -1]; generate_steered(model, prompt, v, alpha, layer) with model.hooks(fwd_hooks=[...]); sweep(alphas) -> DataFrame of sentiment rate, perplexity, CI per alpha; random control vector with v_rand.norm() == v.norm().
receipt: alpha=0 hooked output == unhooked output for a fixed seed; sentiment rate at alpha=8 exceeds alpha=0 with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs over 100 samples; norm-matched random vector effect is within the alpha=0 CI.
gotchas: Adding the vector to the prompt positions too changes results versus adding only on generated positions, decide and report it; the residual norm grows with depth so the same alpha means different things at different layers, scale alpha by the mean resid norm; forgetting to remove hooks leaves the model steered for the next experiment.
interview_q: How would you show a steering vector is meaningful and not just noise? Sweep the coefficient, measure the target behavior with confidence intervals, compare to a norm-matched random vector, and track a fluency metric to see where the intervention breaks the model.
explainer: We take two prompts that differ in one idea. I love you on the left, I hate you on the right.
We read the residual stream at layer six for both and subtract. The difference is our steering vector.
Averaging over many such pairs cleans it up. Noise from individual prompts cancels out.
Now a neutral prompt runs through the model, and at layer six we add the vector on every new token.
Small coefficient, the story turns warmer. Bigger coefficient, it turns gushing.
Too big, and the text falls apart. Perplexity shoots up at the same point.
A random vector of the same size barely moves anything. That is how we know the direction is real.
